item.title: Trump Taps Stephen Miller to Replace Wiles as Chief of Staff
item.description:
President Trump announced that he is tapping longtime aide Stephen Miller as his next White House chief of staff and that current chief of staff Susie Wiles will move to his political operation on November 9th. The move comes after Republicans suffered major losses in the midterm elections, losing control of both chambers of congress and limiting the party heading into President Trump's final two years in office. Bloomberg's Jeff Mason and Kailey Leinz report. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Kok Leong Chan

item.title: The Macro Implications of the Blue Tsunami
item.description:
We don't need to tell you that the midterm elections were historic: The Democrats won bigger than even they imagined. But as the dust settles, an open question we are puzzling over is the market's ongoing reaction to this massive political sea change. Democratic control of Congress — and control over a number of formerly red statehouses like Texas and Iowa — will influence everything from the composition of the FOMC to data center construction. And what we're seeing right now, with stocks like Tesla and SpaceX tumbling, is a direct response to these conditions. To get a better sense of this macro moment, we turn to Odd Lots regular, Employ America's executive director Skanda Amarnath to talk about how the midterms will influence the Fed's battle with inflation, Elon Musk's political instincts, and what a Democratic majority means for the market, tariffs, and AI. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Global Tech Selloff Deepens as US Midterms Trigger AI Fears
item.description:
Bloomberg Daybreak Europe is your essential morning viewing to stay ahead. Live from Brussels, we set the agenda for your day, catching you up with overnight markets news from the US and Asia. And we'll tell you what matters for investors in Europe, giving you insight before trading begins. The global stock selloff worsened in Asia, with a regional benchmark dropping the most in more than a year, on concern the US will tighten regulations on the AI industry after Democrats’ decisive election win. European futures also headed lower. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is weighing whether to leave the Trump administration, people familiar with the matter said, as he considers his next moves following Republicans’ midterm elections wipeout this week. Rubio dismissed the report, telling the New York Times that he didn’t know where the information came from. Today's guests: Stéphane Boujnah, Euronext, CEO; Ellie Henderson, Investec, Economist. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Siri AI's Biggest Upgrade Yet + John Ternus's First Apple Earnings Call
item.description:
Apple is finally bringing some of Siri's most ambitious AI capabilities to the iPhone. In this episode of Power On, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman and Vlad Savov break down the major changes coming with iOS 27.3, including Siri's new ability to control apps, carry out complex tasks and coordinate actions across multiple applications. They discuss how these improvements compare with AI agents from OpenAI and Meta, and why Apple still has a long way to go. Plus, Mark and Vlad analyze John Ternus's first earnings call as Apple's CEO, the company's strong iPhone sales, concerns about slowing growth and profit margins, and why more price increases could be coming. They also examine Apple's AI rollout in China and the privacy implications of new always-listening Apple Watch features. Have a question for Mark? Email us at poweron@bloomberg.net or join the Power On Discord Subscribe to the Power On Newsletter at https://www.bloomberg.com/poweron (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Omar El Chmouri and Laura Gardner Cuesta

item.title: An Election Day Special With Nate Silver
item.description:
Nate Silver tells us he is calling this midterms the “rock and a hard place election” — the background conditions are great for Democrats to win both the House and the Senate, but for that to come to pass, the party has to pull off some things that haven't happened in generations, like winning Texas. To believe that will happen requires a certain leap of faith, which is anathema to pollsters. Still, the polls generally believe Democrats are favored, but many professional pollsters would end up with egg on their face if the night does not go that way. Silver — the founder of Silver Bulletin — joins us today to discuss why popular narratives around polling error are wrong, prediction markets, why he doesn't think AI will replace pollsters, and what he is paying attention to tonight as the polls close. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: The $300 Billion Structured Notes Market Is Booming
item.description:
The structured products business in the US has gotten very large recently — on track to hit $300 billion in sales this year. What was once an opaque financial product is getting a lot more attention. So what are structured products, exactly, and how are they influencing the economy? In short, structured products are basically a fusion of a bank IOU with a derivative product, but that underplays how complex they are and how they are shaping market dynamics. On this episode, we speak with Alex Micalizzi, who is the international head of equity structured notes at Nomura, and he gives us what might be the clearest explanation of how structured products are created, how they work, and why sales in structured products has grown so much in the last year. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Trump Can Drive Turnout on Both Sides: Taylor
item.description:
Jessica Taylor, Senate and Governors editor for The Cook Political Report, says President Donald Trump is needed on the campaign trail to drive Republican turnout, but making the midterms about himself could also motivate Democrats and independents to vote against his party. Taylor says Cook moved Florida's Senate race from Solid Republican to Likely Republican because it expects a single-digit contest and says Florida could offer an early indication of how Republicans are performing nationally. Taylor says some states could produce different results in their gubernatorial and Senate races and that the bigger question in the closing days is which voters ultimately turn out. She speaks with Joe Mathieu and Kailey Leinz on Bloomberg’s "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Killin Says Affordability Is Driving Colorado Race
item.description:
Jessica Killin, Colorado Democratic Congressional candidate, says affordability is the central concern she hears from voters and argues Congress needs to take back its power on tariffs and the war with Iran. Killin says tariffs are raising costs for small businesses and calls for Congress to play a larger role in pursuing a longer-term agreement with Iran while also addressing housing and health care. Killin says her Army and private-sector background gives her an understanding of how to help the economy grow and calls questions over her Colorado residency a nonissue after a judge dismissed the case. She speaks with Joe Mathieu and Kailey Leinz on Bloomberg’s "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Rakteem Katakey and Elena Mazneva

item.title: UK Chancellor John Healey Defends Budget Plans
item.description:
Bloomberg Daybreak Europe is your essential morning viewing to stay ahead. Live from Brussels, we set the agenda for your day, catching you up with overnight markets news from the US and Asia. And we'll tell you what matters for investors in Europe, giving you insight before trading begins. On today's show, the tech rally stalled as Google parent Alphabet slumped 10% post-market on concerns its massive AI spending isn't paying off. Samsung also fell after it withheld its shareholder payout plans until January 2027. The US Federal Reserve held interest rates as policymakers look for more data on the inflation outlook. And the UK Chancellor has told Bloomberg his Budget will tackle the deficit. John Healey unveiled a modest maiden budget, with measures to bring in £6.6 billion in additional revenue by fiscal year 2030-31. Today's guest: Rufaro Chiriseri, RBC Wealth Management, Head of Fixed Income. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: What Wall Street Really Thinks About the AI Trade Now
item.description:
It has been a big week for the AI trade — we've seen wobbles in the market, many of them in response to headlines like the Anthropic S-1 and earnings from the hyperscalers (Oracle, Microsoft, etc.). So what does Wall Street make of all the news, and how are they processing an increasing sense that the laws of the economy barely apply to AI? Today, we speak with Alexander 'Alty' Altmann, global head of equities tactical strategies at Barclays, and he helps us make sense of how Wall Street really feels about the AI trade right now. We also talk about the KOSPI-fication of the S&P 500, if there are any historical precedents for the capex going into the AI buildout, and if AI is really immune to interest rates. (Source: Bloomberg)

The shares closed Monday at a record low as the airline grapples with cash burn and elevated oil prices. - Boeing (BA) shares are on the move after posted a quarterly loss after higher costs affected its commercial-jet business. The company's total revenue grew about 4% to $24.19 billion, driven in part by stronger sales from its defense, space and security business. Boeing generated cash despite the loss, and its 737 program is progressing toward stabilized production at 47 jets a month. (Source: Bloomberg)

Can South Africa’s City of Gold turn itself around? On this episode of Next Africa, Jennifer Zabasajja examines the financial pressures and political instability behind Johannesburg’s decline, and whether upcoming local elections could help change its course. Business Leadership South Africa CEO Busi Mavuso explains why companies are being forced to work around failing public services. Ninety One founder and CEO Hendrik du Toit discusses the investment needed to rebuild the city, while Eskom CEO Dan Marokane explains how the utility moved from rolling blackouts to excess generating capacity—and why Johannesburg still faces outages. Plus, Bloomberg South Africa Bureau Chief Alex Parker assesses the city’s infrastructure backlog and prospects for recovery. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: AI Agents Are Already Changing the Price of Goods
item.description:
It's obvious that things are getting more expensive, and there are plenty of reasons behind the surge in prices — whether it's wars or inflation or companies padding their profit margins. But with the release of AI agents like Meta's Muse, tech companies are promising consumers that agents will start saving them tons of money by finding the best deals. According to today's guest, Lindsay Owens, the history of price gouging does not bode well for claims that things might get cheaper because of new technology, and research conducted by her think tank Groundwork Collaborative shows that a number of consumer facing agents end up serving customers more expensive items after learning more about their financial situation. Her new book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price — and What That Means for Your Wallet gets into the history of how companies got away with charging more for their goods, through means like data collection and surveillance. (Source: Bloomberg)

Selig says he's disappointed Congress did not pass the Clarity Act which would have set up new rules for the crypto industry. Selig also says the agency is scrutinizing oil market trading related to President Donald Trump's announcements about the war in Iran. He speaks to Bloomberg's Tyler Kendall at the Agricultural Commodity Futures Conference in Overland Park, Kansas. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Bloomberg

item.title: The Forgotten Godmother of Economic Literature
item.description:
In 1776, the field of economics was born with the publication of Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations. Among the book's earliest readers was a Regency-era novelist named Maria Edgeworth. In her time, Edgeworth was one of the most famous literary figures in England, and she smuggled into her stories economic concepts and debates around rent seeking, the idea of productive labor, and so on. These works were enormously influential and they helped expose a generation to practical applications of Smith's theories. Jeanna Smialek, a veteran Fed reporter and the Brussels bureau chief at The New York Times, thinks Edgeworth's name needs to be placed back in the pantheon of economic history. Today, we discuss Edgeworth's friendly debates with the likes of Thomas Malthus and David Ricardo, how the Irish potato famine reshaped economic thought, and how Edgeworth used the novel form to educate the masses on the value of economics. (Source: Bloomberg)

Lehman says farmers have not felt that an Iowa voice has been standing up for them in Washington and says that while farmers need relief, temporary measures do not address the underlying causes of their financial strain. Gower said mine supply is expected to fall this year, with further risks next year from project recoveries and potential strikes in Chile and the U.S. Other possible supports include continued tariff-related stockpiling, stronger AI demand and Chinese stimulus.
